item.title: #3583079: A denied Explorer execute submission reports an internal exception message and still offers the Execute button
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal unknown (0)
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583079 · 1 contributor · 2 comments

Summary

When a user without the right permission tried to execute a tool from the Tool Explorer, the denial page still showed an Execute button, and pressing it produced a second, confusing error exposing an internal developer-facing exception message rather than just the plain access-denied notice. This fix ensures that a denied execution page no longer offers an Execute button, and that submitting a denied (or otherwise un-run) tool reports only the original denial message instead of layering a cryptic internal error on top of it.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

The root cause was that ToolExecuteForm::buildForm() unconditionally appended the Execute submit button after the plugin form ran, even when the plugin form's access() check had denied execution and returned only denial markup (access_denied). Separately, ToolExecuteForm::submitForm() unconditionally called $tool->getResult() after submission, but ToolBase::getResult() throws a BadMethodCallException if the tool's execute() method never ran, which is exactly the case on a denied submission.

The fix adds two guards in modules/tool_explorer/src/Form/ToolExecuteForm.php: buildForm() now only adds the actions.submit Execute button when $form['access_denied'] is not set, and submitForm() now checks $tool->hasResult() before calling getResult(), returning early (leaving the plugin form's own denial message as the only reported error) when there is no result to retrieve. Kernel test coverage was added in ExecuteToolPluginFormTest (testDeniedPageOffersNoExecuteButton and testDeniedSubmitReportsOnce) to assert the denial page has no submit action and that a denied submission produces exactly one error message with no ::execute() exception text. The issue notes this flaw predates #3583077 (declared-permission pre-checks) but that change made the denial path routine to reach rather than a rare edge case.

item.title: #3583077: Invokers must check the declared permission before processing caller input
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Major task
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583077 · 1 contributor · 2 comments

Summary

The Tool module's built-in ways of running a tool (the tool:run Drush command, the Explorer's execute form, and the AI connector used by tool_ai_connector) previously processed the caller's input, resolving entity handles, running coercions and refiners, before checking whether the caller was even allowed to run the tool. For a tool that declares a permission (added in #3583064), that meant an unauthorized caller's attacker-controlled values were still touched before being denied. These invokers now check the declared permission first and deny immediately, before touching any input, falling back to the existing access() check afterward as before.

Impact

Affects site owners.

  • Security: tool:run, the Explorer's execute form, and the AI connector now call ToolManager::checkPermission() to deny a caller lacking the tool's declared permission before any of the caller's input is parsed, transformed, or validated, instead of only after resolving handles and running refiners on it.

Technical details

Each in-tree invoker now calls the static ToolManager::checkPermission($definition, $account) before setting any caller-supplied value. ToolRunCommand::executeTool() checks it right after fetching the plugin definition, before createInstance() or setInputValue() runs; ExecuteToolPluginForm::buildConfigurationForm() checks it before building any widgets from refined definitions, and submitConfigurationForm() checks it again before extracting submitted values; tool_ai_connector's ToolPluginBase::execute() checks it before forwarding any LLM-provided context value. All three still call access() afterward as the real execution gate, since checkPermission() is definition-only and cheap, while access() also runs the tool's own values-dependent checkAccess().

Denial reporting was consolidated so a caller cannot tell which stage denied: ToolRunCommand gained a private accessDeniedMessage() helper and ToolPluginBase gained recordAccessDenial(), both now shared between the permission pre-check and the access() check.

The invoker contract is now documented in docs/developers/index.md under "Invoking a tool": check the declared permission, set inputs, validate, call access(), then execute(). It also specifies what each stage may reveal: nothing before the permission check passes (no transform events, no violation text, no schema echo), and only shape feedback (schema-based violations, correctable-failure schema echo) after it, since the schema is already advertised at that gate. docs/developers/creating-a-tool.md now explains that a value-independent access rule belongs in permission, not checkAccess(), precisely because only the former denies before input processing. Kernel tests (DeclaredPermissionDenialTest, additions to ToolRunCommandTest and ExecuteToolPluginFormTest) assert the denial happens before any input transform event fires.</technical> <parameter name="upgrade">Custom invokers (the MCP bridge, other external callers) should follow the documented ordering to get the same early-denial behavior:

$definition = $tool_manager->getDefinition($tool_id);
$permission_access = ToolManager::checkPermission($definition, $account);
if (!$permission_access->isAllowed()) {
  // Report the denial the same way an access() denial is reported.
  return;
}

// Now safe to process caller input:
$tool = $tool_manager->createInstance($tool_id, [], $invoker);
$tool->setInputValue($name, $value);
// ... validate, then:
$access = $tool->access(NULL, TRUE);

Keep a value-independent access rule in a tool's permission rather than its checkAccess() override, since only permission is checked before input processing.

item.title: #3583071: Inputs and outputs declared with data type "map" are advertised as strings on Drupal 10 and 11.0
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Major bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583071 · 1 contributor · 5 comments

Summary

On Drupal 10 and 11.0, Tool API's JSON Schema generator incorrectly advertised any tool input or output declared with the plain map data type (as opposed to the dedicated map classes) as a string instead of an object. This mismatch broke tools in practice: a server or client that validates arguments or results against the advertised schema, such as mcp_server, would reject the object the tool actually needs or returns. The tool_belt module alone declares 28 such plain map inputs and outputs, so this affected a substantial share of real tools. The fix makes plain map definitions advertise as objects consistently on every supported core version, matching the behavior already present on Drupal 11.1+.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

The root cause was in ContextDefinitionNormalizer::getNormalizationSchema(). A data_type: 'map' declared on the dedicated MapInputDefinition/MapOutputDefinition classes (subclasses of MapDataDefinition) was already handled correctly, taking the map branch that builds {"type": "object", ...}. But the same map data type declared on a plain InputDefinition or OutputDefinition is just a DataDefinition, so it fell through to the typed-data branch, which asks the serializer for the json_schema of a Map typed-data object. On cores before 11.1, that request is handled by LegacyTypedDataNormalizer (registered at a higher priority than MapDefinitionNormalizer in tool.services.yml), which has no arm for Map and returns an empty array, which then falls back to advertising {"type": "string"}.

The fix extends the existing map branch's condition from $object instanceof MapDataDefinition to also match $object->getDataType() === 'map', mirroring how the list data type is already special-cased a few lines above it. When the object isn't a MapDataDefinition, there are no property definitions to iterate, so applyMapConstraintSchema() and the empty-properties object logic now apply uniformly to plain maps too. A new test, PlainMapSchemaTest, asserts that a plain map definition and its MapInputDefinition/MapOutputDefinition equivalent normalize to identical schemas, including under a Count constraint that bounds minProperties/maxProperties.

The issue notes other data types (binary, language_reference) may hit the same legacy-path string fallback on Drupal 10.6 but leaves deciding whether they need their own arm as a remaining task, not addressed by this change.

item.title: #3583073: A map output whose keys are 0, 1, 2… is sent as a JSON array, so it fails its object schema
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583073 · 1 contributor · 5 comments

Summary

The Tool module lets a plugin declare an output as a free-form "map", advertised in its schema as a JSON object. If the PHP array a tool returned for that output happened to have sequential integer keys starting at 0 (['a', 'b'], or [0 => 'x']), PHP's json_encode() wrote it as a JSON array instead of an object, because PHP cannot distinguish a list from a map by its contents alone. The result then failed validation against the tool's own advertised output schema. This affected MCP clients and other code that validates a tool's structuredContent, as well as Drush's tool:run --json output. The fix makes every non-multiple map serialize as a JSON object regardless of its keys, matching what the schema promises.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

The conversion happens in OutputTypeCoercionSubscriber::onOutputTransform(). Previously it only wrapped a map value in \ArrayObject when the value was exactly [], relying on the fact that json_encode(new \ArrayObject()) writes {}. The fix widens the check to \is_array($value) && \array_is_list($value) && $definition->getDataType() === 'map' && !$definition->isMultiple(), wrapping any list-keyed array (empty or not) in new \ArrayObject($value). Since json_encode() always writes an \ArrayObject as an object, the wrapped value now matches the object schema type whatever its keys. A map with declared properties has string keys and is therefore never a list, so it still gets walked by RecursiveToolValueTransformSubscriber as before; only free-form, list-keyed maps take the new path.

Because the formatted value can now arrive as an \ArrayObject instead of a plain array even when non-empty, two call sites needed updating: ToolOutputTrait::referenceEntities() now unwraps an \ArrayObject via getArrayCopy(), replaces entities inside it, and re-wraps it, and ToolRunCommand::serializeOutputs() comments and handling were updated accordingly (it already passed \ArrayObject values through). Test coverage was added via a new ListKeyedMapOutputTool fixture exercising a top-level map, a map declared via the plain OutputDefinition, a map nested as a declared property of another map, and a list of maps, plus assertions in AdvertisedOutputSchemaConformanceTest and ToolRunCommandTest.

item.title: #3583072: The schema of an optional enum input allows null in its type but not in its enum, so null is rejected
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Major bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583072 · 1 contributor · 5 comments

Summary

Optional tool inputs that are restricted to a fixed set of values (via Symfony's Choice/AllowedValues constraints, a derived PluginExists enum, or an IdenticalTo constant) advertised a JSON Schema that contradicted itself: the schema's type allowed null, but its enum or const keyword did not, so any JSON Schema validator rejected a null value even though Tool API itself accepted it for an optional input. In practice, MCP clients validate tools/call arguments against the published schema before the call ever reaches the tool, so a model sending null for an optional enum input it didn't want to set (ordinary, expected behavior) got its call rejected with a JSON-RPC error. This is now fixed: an optional input's schema lists null as an allowed enum value (or widens a const to an enum of the constant and null), so the published schema matches what the tool actually accepts.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: Optional inputs with a Choice/AllowedValues/PluginExists constraint now advertise null as a listed enum value, and an optional IdenticalTo-constrained input's const is widened to enum: [<const>, null], so the published JSON Schema matches what Tool API already accepted for those inputs.

Technical details

The fix lives in ContextDefinitionNormalizer::allowNullValue(), called from the optional-input branch that already appends the null type (or oneOf null branch on Drupal 11.1+). When the input is optional and not excluded by NotNull/non-nullable NotBlank, the new method widens the value keywords to agree with the type: if const is set it becomes enum: [<const>, null]; if enum is set and lacks null, null is appended. This covers both the legacy type: [string, null] array and the newer oneOf composition without per-core branching, and applies uniformly to Choice/AllowedValues-derived enums, PluginExists-derived enums, and IdenticalTo-derived const values.

A separate but related gap was closed in SchemaToolsPropertyConverter::prepareAiPropertySchema(), used when rendering schemas for AI providers that require a flattened (non-union) type: since that flattening drops the null type member, any null left in enum would then mismatch the flattened type and be rejected by strict providers, so it now strips null from enum (and drops enum entirely if that empties it) after flattening.

Test coverage was updated accordingly: InputSchemaMatrixTest's enum_string/enum_integer expectations now include null, RicherSchemaEmissionTest checks that an optional IdenticalTo widens const to an enum with null (while a required one keeps a plain const), and a new AdvertisedSchemaAcceptanceTest::testNullIsAcceptedWhereTheSchemaOffersIt() iterates every discovered tool's optional inputs whose schema allows the null type and asserts both that a JSON Schema validator accepts a null value and that Tool API's own validateInputValue() raises no violation for it, closing the gap that the prior sampled round-trip test never exercised the null branch.

item.title: #3583067: Decimal and string coercion of JSON numbers adds float noise to values with an integer part
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583067 · 1 contributor · 5 comments

Summary

The Tool module's coercion layer, which converts JSON numbers coming from AI tool calls into Drupal field values (and back), was adding binary floating-point noise to any number with an integer part. For example, sending 1234.567 to a decimal or plain text field came back as 1234.56700000000001, and 99999.99 came back as 99999.99000000000524. Decimal fields usually hid this on save because core rounds to the field's configured scale, but plain string fields had nothing to round the noise away, so the corrupted value could be stored as-is. This fix makes the formatter emit the number exactly as given (up to the precision a double can represent), so values round-trip cleanly through tools that set, read, or preview field values before saving.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

The bug was in DecimalStringTrait::formatDecimalString(), used by both InputTypeCoercionSubscriber (for string and decimal inputs) and OutputTypeCoercionSubscriber (for decimal outputs holding a float). It formatted every float with a fixed 14 decimal places via \number_format($value, 14, '.', ''), under the mistaken assumption that this matched PHP's precision setting. PHP's precision counts significant digits, not decimal places, and a double only reliably holds about 15 to 17 significant digits, so once a value had an integer part, 14 decimal places reached past what the double actually stores and printed the binary rounding error.

The fix computes the decimal places needed to land on 15 significant digits: $decimals = \max(0, 14 - (int) \floor(\log10(\abs($value)))), then formats and trims trailing zeros as before. Zero is special-cased to return '0' directly. Below 1e15 this reproduces the value as written (1234.567, 99999.99, 12345678.123) while still collapsing genuine binary artifacts like 0.1 + 0.2 down to 0.3. At 1e15 and above, every integer digit of the double is still spelled out without exponent notation, so artifacts past that point can still appear, consistent with the corrected docblock.

Matrix test cases were added to InputCoercionMatrixTest for plain_decimal and plain_string inputs, and a new OutputCoercionMatrixTest was added covering the equivalent decimal output cases, all asserting the exact strings callers should see. This bug was introduced alongside the decimal/string input coercion work in #3582983 and the decimal output coercion work in #3583030.

item.title: #3583069: Align map validation with JSON Schema: a required map may be empty
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal task
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583069 · 1 contributor · 13 comments

Summary

Tool API publishes a JSON Schema for every tool input and output, but until now its own validation disagreed with that schema for maps: a required map was documented as accepting {} but validation rejected it as if it were NULL. This broke real tools, for example canvas_get_component_schema in canvas_tools failed for every component without slots or props because that output is a legitimately empty map. This issue aligns map validation with the schema, the same way a companion issue (#3583040) previously did for lists: a required map may now be empty, and only an explicit NULL is rejected. Tools that had to declare such maps as optional as a workaround can go back to declaring them required.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: A required map input or output now accepts an empty value ({}/[]); only NULL is rejected. Declare NotBlank or Count on the map to require at least one property, which now publishes as minProperties in the JSON Schema (mirroring minItems for lists).

Technical details

The fix mirrors the list treatment from #3583040: EffectiveDataDefinition::createFrom() no longer marks a MapDataDefinition as required (alongside lists), so core typed data adds no NotNull constraint to it and an empty map passes. Required is still enforced for NULL: TypedInputsTrait and TypedOutputsTrait explicitly reject a NULL value for a required list or map via ValueViolationsTrait::validateListNotNull(). Required properties of a map stay protected on a different path: TypedInputsTrait::validateInputValue() and TypedOutputsTrait::validateOutputValue() walk a map's declared properties directly and report a missing required property before typed-data validation runs, which is what keeps core's known gap (an empty map's properties are never validated, drupal.org #3256536) from reopening.

A related bug in the "multiple" to list conversion was fixed alongside this: ListDefinitionBase::splitMultipleConstraints() previously promoted a NotNull or non-nullable NotBlank found among a multiple's item-level constraints up to the converted list itself, implicitly making the list not empty. Since a multiple's constraints only ever bind its items, that promotion was wrong and is removed; only Count still moves to the list.

To let an author still require a genuinely non-empty list or map, NotBlank (or Count) declared directly on the list or map now normalizes through ContextDefinitionNormalizer::applyListConstraintSchema() and applyMapConstraintSchema() into minItems: 1 or minProperties: 1 in the published schema, and is enforced the same way at validation time.</technical> <parameter name="upgrade">If a tool declared a map input or output as optional purely to work around the old empty-map rejection, it can be declared required again:

'settings' => new MapOutputDefinition(
  label: new TranslatableMarkup('Settings'),
  description: new TranslatableMarkup('The settings.'),
  required: TRUE,
),

If a map or list must never be empty, declare that explicitly instead of relying on required:

'nodes' => new ListInputDefinition(
  label: new TranslatableMarkup('Nodes'),
  description: new TranslatableMarkup('The nodes to export.'),
  constraints: ['NotBlank' => []],
  item_definition: new EntityInputDefinition('entity:node', ...),
),

NotBlank publishes as minItems: 1 for a list or minProperties: 1 for a map; Count can set an explicit minimum/maximum instead.

item.title: #3583064: Declare permissions on a tool definition for static access checks
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal feature request
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583064 · 1 contributor · 4 comments

Summary

The Tool module (an API for defining executable "tools", used for things like AI agent/MCP integrations) lets a tool plugin declare the permission an account needs to run it, directly on the #[Tool] attribute, instead of writing that check by hand inside checkAccess(). A new static check on the tool manager can test that declared permission against an account straight from the tool's definition, without creating an instance of the tool. This means a picker or a listing that advertises many tools to a user can filter out the ones they cannot run cheaply and with a cacheable result, rather than having to instantiate every tool and supply input values just to find out. Tools that declare no permission behave exactly as before.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: ToolBase::checkAccess() is no longer abstract: it now has a default implementation that allows access when the tool declares a permission, and ToolBase::access() composes the new permission check with checkAccess() via andIf() instead of calling checkAccess() alone.
  • New API: #[Tool(permission: ...)] attribute parameter and ToolManager::checkPermission(ToolDefinition $definition, AccountInterface $account) let code check a tool's required permission from its definition alone, without instantiating the plugin.

Technical details

The attribute gains a permission string parameter, exposed on ToolDefinition::getPermission()/setPermission() (derivers can set it per derivative). It follows the syntax of a route's _permission requirement: names joined with , are all required, names joined with + are OR'd, and mixing both operators in one string is rejected. The actual implementation differs from the issue's original proposal of a permissions array plus a checkPermissionAccess() method: what landed is a single route-style string and a static ToolManager::checkPermission(ToolDefinition $definition, AccountInterface $account): AccessResultInterface, which parses the string and delegates to AccessResult::allowedIfHasPermissions(), carrying user.permissions cacheability.

ToolBase::access() now runs this permission check first, short-circuiting before input resolution/validation, then andIfs it with the result of checkAccess(). checkAccess() is no longer abstract: its default implementation just allows when the definition declares a permission, so a purely permission-gated tool needs no override at all; an override still runs and its result is combined with the permission check, so it can only add restrictions, not bypass the declared permission. A bare bool returned from checkAccess() is wrapped with setCacheMaxAge(0) before being combined, since a bool carries no cacheability metadata of its own.

ToolManager::processDefinition() adds two discovery-time guards, thrown as InvalidPluginDefinitionException when the plugin cache rebuilds: a permission string mixing , and + fails immediately, and a tool that declares no permission and overrides neither checkAccess() nor access() (i.e. has no access rule at all) is rejected, replacing what used to be a hard PHP fatal from the removed abstract method. drush tool:info and the Tool Explorer UI both print the declared permission and flag names that match no defined permission.

Upgrade

A tool whose access rule is only a permission check can drop its checkAccess() override and declare it on the attribute instead:

#[Tool(
  id: 'my_tool',
  // ...
  permission: 'administer users',
)]
final class MyTool extends ToolBase {
  // No checkAccess() override needed.
}

Multiple required permissions: permission: 'administer users,access administration pages'. Any-of: permission: 'operate test tools+audit test tools'. An override of checkAccess() no longer needs to re-check the declared permission itself: access() already requires it before checkAccess() runs, and the override's result is combined with andIf().

item.title: #3583062: Required means present for lists and maps; an explicit NotBlank carries non-empty
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal task
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583062 · 1 contributor · 4 comments

Summary

The Tool module's rule for whether an empty list ([]) or map ({}) satisfies a required input or output has been made consistent. Before this, behavior disagreed depending on how the definition was declared: a required list converted from the older "multiple" style rejected an empty array while a hand-declared required list accepted it, and different schema consumers (the tool-native schema, the MCP bridge, and the ai module's context bridge) disagreed about whether an empty array was even allowed. The rule now applied everywhere, for both lists and maps, and for both inputs and outputs, is that required means the value must be present and not NULL; an empty array or object still counts as present. A tool author who needs to guarantee a non-empty list or map has to say so explicitly, with a NotBlank or Count constraint.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: A required list or map input or output no longer rejects, or advertises as non-empty, an empty array or object by itself; add NotBlank or Count to require a non-empty value, which is what is now advertised as minItems/minProperties.

Technical details

ListDefinitionBase::splitMultipleConstraints() (src/TypedData/ListDefinitionBase.php) no longer infers a list-level NotNull from a converted multiple's NotNull or NotBlank; it moves only Count to the list, leaving every other constraint, NotBlank included, bound to the item. EffectiveDataDefinition::createFrom(), which builds the typed-data definition TypedInputsTrait/TypedOutputsTrait actually validate against, now withholds the required flag from maps the same way it already did for lists, so typed data's automatic NotNull default constraint never reaches a list or map's effective definition. TypedInputsTrait::validateInputValue() rejects an explicit NULL for a required list or map itself (via validateListNotNull()) while letting an empty array or object through.

On the schema side, ContextDefinitionNormalizer::applyListConstraintSchema() and the new applyMapConstraintSchema() (src/Normalizer/ContextDefinitionNormalizer.php) only emit minItems/minProperties: 1 when the definition carries an explicit NotBlank, not merely because it is required, removing the tool-side inference that a required multiple implies a non-empty array. tool_ai_connector's ToolContextDefinitionTrait::toListDefinition() was updated the same way: a list-level NotBlank is treated as author-declared only, never something the ai-context adapter infers.

This settles the "open question" the issue raised about maps by extending the existing list/output rule (required means present, not empty, per the earlier #3583040) uniformly to maps and to the input direction, rather than adopting the input-specific "reject empty" rule this issue's body had proposed.

Upgrade

To require a non-empty list or map input (or output), declare NotBlank (or Count for bounds) explicitly; required by itself no longer implies it:

'nodes' => new ListInputDefinition(
  label: new TranslatableMarkup('Nodes'),
  description: new TranslatableMarkup('The nodes to export.'),
  constraints: ['NotBlank' => []],
  item_definition: new EntityInputDefinition('entity:node', ...),
),

This is advertised in the generated JSON Schema as minItems: 1 (or minProperties: 1 for a map), rather than being inferred from required.

item.title: #3583047: tool:run --json prints an entity output as its full field array, including the password hash
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583047 · 1 contributor · 9 comments

Summary

The tool:run Drush command could print an entity output's entire field array, in both JSON and plain text mode. For a user entity this included pass, the hashed password, which could end up visible in a terminal, a log, or an AI agent's transcript. The command now prints entities only as a small reference (entity type, ID, UUID, and label) instead of dumping their fields, so no field data, secret or otherwise, leaks through tool:run output.

Impact

Affects site owners.

  • Security: Fixed exposure of entity field values, including a user's password hash, in drush tool:run output (both --json and text modes).

Technical details

The fix adds a referenceEntities() helper to ToolOutputTrait, used from both ToolRunCommand::serializeOutputs() (the --json path) and ToolOutputTrait::formatOutputValue() (the plain-text path). Any value that is an EntityInterface is replaced with an array of entity_type, id, uuid, and label (taken from the entity's own label(), so no direct field access happens); arrays are walked recursively so a multiple entity output has each item replaced too. This closes a gap left by #3583035, which switched ToolRunCommand to getFormattedResult()->getContextValues() but only replaces entities with handles for invokers that declare InvokerCapability::EntitiesAsHandles; DrushInvoker declares none, so the formatted result still held the raw entity object, and the previous toArray()/get_class() fallbacks either dumped every field or leaked nothing useful.

The change is deliberately scoped to the reference shape described in the issue rather than waiting for real CLI entity handles (tracked separately in #3582977), which will eventually replace this reference representation. Test coverage is a new account_output_tool test plugin returning a user both as a single output and as a multiple output, with a kernel test asserting the password hash and the pass key never appear in either output mode.

item.title: #3588984: Not Drupal 12 compatible
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal unknown (0)
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3588984 · 1 contributor · 6 comments

Summary

Installing this module into a Drupal 12 site previously failed outright: Composer could not resolve dependencies because the module's composer.json pinned Symfony Console/Filesystem/Yaml to versions 6 or 7, while Drupal 12 requires Symfony 8. This is now fixed, the module installs cleanly on Drupal 12.

Impact

Affects site owners.

  • Requirements: composer.json now allows symfony/console, symfony/filesystem, and symfony/yaml ^8.0 in addition to ^6.0/^7.0, so the package installs alongside Drupal 12's Symfony 8 dependency.

Technical details

The fix widens the version constraints for symfony/console, symfony/filesystem, and symfony/yaml in composer.json to also accept ^8.0. That alone wasn't sufficient because Symfony Console 8 removed Application::add() in favor of addCommand() (introduced in 7.4), while the Console phar bundled inside Composer itself is still 5.4 and only has add(). AiBestPracticesApplication's constructor now checks method_exists($this, 'addCommand') and calls whichever method is available, so the same code works whether the runtime Console is old or new. item.title: #3582967: Harden the 'administer tool' permission
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal task
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3582967 · 1 contributor · 7 comments

Summary

The Tool Explorer's administer tool permission, which controls execution of arbitrary Tool plugins (including entity creation, modification, and deletion), previously had only a bare title with no warning that it was a sensitive, security-relevant permission. It is now flagged as restricted in Drupal's permissions UI, and its description explicitly warns that granting it allows executing tools that can change site data and configuration. A new view tool information permission lets roles browse the list of registered tools and view their input, output, and configuration schemas without being able to run them, so site builders no longer have to grant full execute access just to let someone audit what tools exist.

Affects site owners.

  • Permission change: The administer tool permission is now marked restrict access: true with a warning description; a new view tool information permission grants read-only browsing of Tool Explorer definitions without allowing execution.

Technical details

The fix in tool.permissions.yml adds restrict access: true and a warning description to administer tool, and introduces a second permission, view tool information (also restricted), covering read-only browsing. tool_explorer.routing.yml changes the tool_explorer.list and tool_explorer.view routes' _permission requirement to 'view tool information+administer tool' (either permission grants access), while tool_explorer.execute keeps requiring administer tool alone.

ToolExplorerController::listTools() now builds the row operations conditionally: the view link is always present, but the execute dropbutton link is only added when $this->currentUser()->hasPermission('administer tool') is true. Because the rendered operations now vary by permission, the list render array's #cache was given a user.permissions cache context to avoid serving a cached row with the Execute link to a user who lacks administer tool. A new kernel test, ToolExplorerAccessTest, asserts both permissions are marked restricted, checks route access for anonymous, no-permission, read-only, and administrator accounts, and verifies which operations links appear per role.

Sites that grant administer tool to a role only so users can browse the Tool Explorer without executing tools should switch that role to the new view tool information permission instead:

view tool information:
  title: 'View tool information'
  description: 'Browse tool definitions in Tool Explorer, including input, output, and configuration schemas.'
  restrict access: true

Custom code checking access to the Explorer's list or view routes should account for the new _permission: 'view tool information+administer tool' requirement (either permission suffices), while the execute route still requires administer tool alone.

item.title: #3583060: Structure-reading constraints on a map input throw instead of validating
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Minor bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583060 · 1 contributor · 6 comments

Summary

The Tool module (a contributed module that lets developers define typed, self-contained "tools" callable from Drush, controllers, ECA, AI agents, or MCP servers) had a bug in input validation: a map input (MapInputDefinition) whose author declared a structure-reading constraint, such as Symfony's ComplexData naming one of the map's own declared properties, would crash with an uncaught InvalidArgumentException: Property X is unknown. instead of reporting a normal validation violation. This is now fixed so such constraints validate correctly and report per-property violations as expected. No in-tree or known consumer tool currently declares this kind of constraint, so the practical exposure before this fix was limited to third-party tool authors who did.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

This was the second regression in the same code path. #3583004 split map validation out of core's Context::validate() into a per-property walk, which silently skipped map-level declared constraints (the map counterpart of the list regression fixed in #3583048). #3583028 then restored enforcement of declared constraints, but rebuilt the typed data from a bare createDataDefinition($definition->getDataType()), a map with no properties, so any constraint that reads the map's structure (like ComplexData naming sku) found the property "unknown" and threw outside any catch.

The fix, in TypedInputsTrait::validateDeclaredConstraints(), builds the typed data for a MapDataDefinition from EffectiveDataDefinition::createFrom($definition) instead, which carries the map's declared properties, while a bare data type is still used for lists (no list-level constraint reads items). Each declared constraint is now run individually through RecursiveValidator::startContext() as a non-root call rather than delegating to a single recursive validate(), so a constraint only visits the members it actually names instead of re-validating every property or descending into entity fields. A new $members_rejected flag lets exceptions from a constraint reading a property whose value already failed its own type check be swallowed (the value is already rejected), while exceptions from genuinely misdeclared constraints, such as ComplexData naming a property the map does not declare, still throw loudly, consistent with the authoring-mistake ruling from #3583048. The regression lineage and the interaction with the earlier required-empty-collection fix (#3583040) and the entity-input change (#3583028) are documented in the updated method docblock.

item.title: #3583035: tool:run sends the PHP output values, not the formatted result
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583035 · 1 contributor · 10 comments

Summary

The tool:run Drush command (used to invoke and inspect Tool module plugins from the command line) was sending raw PHP values instead of the values formatted according to each output's advertised schema. This meant, for example, that a timestamp output showed up as a raw Unix integer (1785606907) instead of the documented date-time string, and an empty map printed its internal \ArrayObject class name instead of {}. The MCP bridge already did this correctly; tool:run was the last in-tree caller reading unformatted values. The command now sends the same formatted output that other invokers, like the MCP bridge, produce.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: ToolRunCommand now emits the formatted output values (matching each output's advertised schema) instead of the tool's raw PHP values; an empty map now serializes as {} instead of an \ArrayObject class name.

Technical details

ToolRunCommand::runTool() previously called $tool->getOutputValues() (guarded by a success check, since output contexts are unset on failure and getOutputValues() throws otherwise) to build the outputs array. It now calls $tool->getFormattedResult()->getContextValues() unconditionally: a failed tool simply carries no output values, so the success guard is removed. getFormattedResult() applies the transform pipeline added in the related timestamp/decimal/datetime coercion work (#3583030), turning entities into handles and spelling timestamps, decimals, and dates the way the schema's date-time etc. types describe.

ToolOutputTrait::formatValue() and ToolRunCommand::serializeOutputs() were both updated to special-case \ArrayObject (used to represent an empty map) so it serializes as {} in both the JSON and human-readable text output paths, rather than falling through to is_object() handling that printed the class name.

Docblocks were added to TypedOutputsInterface::getOutputValue() and getOutputValues() clarifying that these return the tool's raw PHP values (for the tool itself and its tests), and that anything leaving the process should read getFormattedResult() instead. The issue also raised whether to rename these to something like getRawOutputValues()/getFormattedOutputValues() to make the distinction harder to get wrong, but that rename was deferred as a pre-1.0 API decision; only the docblock clarification landed here.

Upgrade

If code or scripts invoke drush tool:run --json and parse specific output fields, expect formatted values rather than raw PHP values, for example:

# Before: raw Unix timestamp
"date": 1785606907

# After: formatted per the output's date-time schema
"date": "2026-08-01T17:55:07+00:00"

Empty map outputs now serialize as {} instead of an ArrayObject class name string.

item.title: #3583030: outputSchema describes a timestamp member as date-time, structuredContent sends integer
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583030 · 1 contributor · 15 comments

Summary

The Tool module builds an MCP outputSchema for each tool's declared output types, but the actual structuredContent payload it sent for a tool's result didn't always match that schema. A timestamp output, for example, was advertised as an RFC 3339 date-time string but sent as a raw Unix integer. Since the MCP spec requires servers to send structured results that conform to the schema, and expects clients to validate against it, this mismatch could make an otherwise-correct tool result get rejected by a compliant client. The fix converts affected values to the format the schema promises before they go out over the wire.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: getFormattedResult() now converts timestamp, decimal, and DateTime-constrained datetime_iso8601 output values, plus empty map outputs, to match the wire format their advertised outputSchema describes (e.g. a Unix timestamp becomes an RFC 3339 string, an empty map becomes {} instead of []); getResult()/getOutputValue() keep returning the original PHP values.

Technical details

The conversion lives in a new OutputTypeCoercionSubscriber, an event subscriber on ToolOutputTransformEvent that runs after invoker-specific subscribers but before the recursive subscriber that walks list/map items, so nested members get the same treatment. It handles four mismatches: a timestamp value is reformatted from a Unix integer to DateTimeInterface::RFC3339 when the active core is 11.1+ (core's schema-aware TimestampNormalizer describes it as a date-time string there; older cores use the module's LegacyTypedDataNormalizer, which describes it as an integer, so it's left alone); a decimal int or float is formatted as a fixed-point string via a new shared DecimalStringTrait (extracted from InputTypeCoercionSubscriber, which already needed the same logic for input coercion); a datetime_iso8601 value carrying the DateTime constraint is reformatted from the offset-less storage spelling (Y-m-d\TH:i:s) to RFC 3339, but only when it matches that exact storage format, anything with an offset or otherwise non-conforming is left untouched; and an empty PHP array for a non-multiple map output is replaced with new \ArrayObject() so it JSON-encodes as {} instead of [].

The new AdvertisedOutputSchemaConformanceTest exercises every discovered tool with schema-conforming sample inputs and validates each formatted output against its normalized schema, plus pins the exact converted spellings so a value that happens to validate but changes meaning (a shifted timezone, a rounded decimal) is still caught.

item.title: #3583040: A required list rejects the empty array its JSON Schema allows
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Version: 1.0.x-dev
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583040 · 1 contributor · 9 comments

Summary

Tool API's validation for required list inputs and outputs previously disagreed with the JSON Schema it publishes. A required list (for example, search results, validation problems, or changed IDs) is advertised in the schema as accepting an empty array, but validation rejected [] with "This value should not be null." This meant a tool could return a valid empty result and still fail its own output validation, or a client following the published schema could send a value the tool would reject anyway. Validation now matches the schema: a required list accepts [], and only NULL (a genuinely missing value) is rejected. Required maps are unaffected: an empty object still fails validation as before.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: A required list input or output (OutputDefinition/InputDefinition with multiple: TRUE, or ListInputDefinition/ListOutputDefinition) now validates successfully when set to an empty array []; only NULL is rejected. Required maps are unchanged and still reject an empty value.

Technical details

The root cause is core's NotNullConstraintValidator, which Tool API inherits as a default constraint whenever a definition is marked required. That validator treats any empty ListInterface or ComplexDataInterface as NULL before checking for nullness, so an empty list tripped the same rejection as a genuinely missing value, even though typed data's "not empty" reading of required diverges from JSON Schema's "key is present" reading.

The fix is in EffectiveDataDefinition: when building the effective typed data definition for validation, a list definition (anything implementing ListDataDefinitionInterface) is no longer marked required, which keeps core's NotNull off of it entirely. TypedInputsTrait::validateInputValue() and TypedOutputsTrait::validateOutputValue() each detect the case that NotNull would otherwise have caught (a NULL value against a required list definition) and explicitly run a NotNull check via the new ValueViolationsTrait::validateListNotNull(), so a NULL list is still rejected with the same message as before. Maps keep their required flag unchanged: they're objects with named properties rather than sequences, and core already skips validating the properties of an empty map (drupal/drupal#3256536), so an empty required map still fails.

A tool that needs at least one item still declares that explicitly with a Count constraint, which the normalizer publishes as minItems in the JSON Schema, for example constraints: ['Count' => ['min' => 1]].</technical> <parameter name="upgrade">If a tool relies on a required list rejecting an empty value, add an explicit Count constraint rather than depending on the removed implicit behavior:

new InputDefinition('entity:node', 'Nodes', 'The nodes to export.', required: TRUE, multiple: TRUE, constraints: ['Count' => ['min' => 1]]);
// {"type": "array", "minItems": 1, ...}

No changes are needed for tools that already treat an empty required list as valid, or for required maps, whose validation is unchanged.

item.title: #3585917: Tool call responses are silently dropped when the handler renders anything (fiber suspension misread as scheduling protocol)
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal unknown (0)
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3585917 · 1 contributor · 9 comments

Summary

In the MCP Server module, a tools/call (and prompts/get, resources/read, completion/complete) request whose handler rendered markup or loaded an entity could complete its work successfully but never send a response back to the client. The client would see nothing, and could wrongly retry the call (creating a duplicate) or assume the operation had failed when it had actually succeeded. This is now fixed: any handler that triggers Drupal's own internal suspension mechanics (rendering, entity loading, theme registry lookups) returns its result normally instead of silently dropping it.

Impact

No upgrade or configuration changes required.

Technical details

The MCP PHP SDK dispatches each request inside a PHP Fiber and interprets any Fiber::suspend() call from within the handler as a ClientGateway operation addressed back to the client (for example, a sampling request). Drupal 10.3+'s own internals use the same mechanism for unrelated purposes: the renderer and EntityStorageBase::loadMultiple() suspend with FiberResumeType::Immediate while resolving placeholders, and the theme registry suspends with no payload on a cold cache. When a tool handler triggered one of these, the SDK misread it as its own scheduling protocol, logged Fiber yielded unexpected payload, and answered the request as text/event-stream instead of application/json, so a JSON-only client never saw the result.

The fix adds Drupal\mcp_server\Capability\FiberShield, which runs the handler in its own inner fiber. It inspects each suspended payload: if it's an array with a type key (a genuine ClientGateway operation), it's re-yielded up to the SDK and the reply is passed back down; anything else (Drupal's internal suspends) is resumed immediately in place, exactly as Drupal's synchronous render path already does. ShieldedReferenceHandler wraps the SDK's ReferenceHandler to cover tools/call, prompts/get, and resources/read, which all flow through it, and ShieldedCompletionProvider wraps each argument-completion provider individually because completion/complete is dispatched directly by the SDK rather than through the reference handler. McpServerFactory wires both decorators in. The issue notes upstream declined to fix this in the SDK itself (php-sdk#505), so the module shields its own dispatch paths instead.

item.title: #3583028: Accept integer map keys and any entity as an entity input
item.description:
• Project: Drupal AI
  • Type: Normal bug report
  • Status: Fixed
  • Discussion: #3583028 · 1 contributor · 23 comments

Summary

The Tool module (a contributed module providing a plugin type for defining typed, self-contained "tools" callable from Drush, controllers, ECA, AI agents, or MCP servers) had two gaps in how it validated the values passed into a tool's inputs. First, an input declared as entity:user_role (or any config entity type) rejected valid Role or NodeType objects, because the check only accepted content entities even though core derives an entity:TYPE data type for config entities too. Second, the entity type and bundle a tool author declared were not actually checked, so a Node passed where an entity:user was expected would pass validation and only fail later, deep inside the tool's own code, with a confusing error. Separately, a config mapping such as system.site's page.403/page.404 keys, which PHP stores as integers, crashed input-definition building entirely. All three cases are fixed: any entity type now satisfies its matching entity:TYPE input, mismatched types or bundles are reported as a proper validation violation naming the input, and integer-keyed mappings work.

Impact

Affects module maintainers.

  • API change: TypedInputsTrait::validateInputValue() now checks an entity input's declared entity type and bundle (and any author-declared constraints) instead of only checking that a value is a ContentEntityInterface; a mismatched entity now produces a validation violation naming the input instead of failing later inside the tool. MapDefinitionBase::setPropertyDefinitions() now accepts integer property names.

Technical details

The entity branch of TypedInputsTrait::validateInputValue() (mirrored in TypedOutputsTrait) used to require $typed_data->getValue() instanceof ContentEntityInterface. It now accepts any EntityInterface, and when the value is an entity, builds a constraint set from the effective definition's dynamic EntityType/Bundle constraints merged with any constraints the input author declared, then runs only those against the entity via the typed data validator, explicitly excluding full entity/field validation and the entity type's own constraints (like EntityChanged). This required generalizing what was validateListConstraints() (list-only) into validateDeclaredConstraints(), used for both lists and maps, since a Count constraint on a map now binds the map's property count rather than being invalid on a scalar. That in turn made Count on a MapInputDefinition surface as minProperties/maxProperties in the generated JSON Schema, via a new ContextDefinitionNormalizer::applyMapConstraintSchema().

MapDefinitionBase::setPropertyDefinitions() now accepts is_int($name) alongside is_string($name), since PHP casts numeric array keys like 403 to integers. Several callers that pass property names into typed parameters (RecursiveToolValueTransformSubscriber, ContextDefinitionNormalizer, MapDefinitionNormalizer, MapAdapter) were updated to cast the key to (string) where a string-typed argument is expected.
